title: Ancient Greek statues weren’t white: they were brightly painted
body: The gleaming white marble we associate with classical sculpture is mostly the work of time. Greek and Roman statues and temples, including the Parthenon, were often painted in strong colors, with patterned clothing and colored eyes. By the time Renaissance artists and 18th-century collectors studied them, most of the paint had weathered away, and bare white stone became the ideal of classical beauty.

slides.heading: Clues in the stone
slides.text: Tiny traces of pigment survive in crevices on many statues and buildings. Modern imaging and chemical analysis can identify which colors were used.

slides.heading: A glowing blue
slides.text: Egyptian blue, a pigment used across the ancient Mediterranean, gives off infrared light when lit, revealing paint on surfaces that look bare to the eye.

steps.label: Imaging and chemical analysis identify them
Egyptian blue glows in infrared under light

slides.heading: Gods in Color
slides.text: Since 2003, the touring exhibition Gods in Color, led by archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann, has shown full-size painted reconstructions of ancient sculpture.

slides.heading: Informed guesses
slides.text: Reconstructions are hypotheses: only traces survive, so the exact shades, shading and finish of the originals remain uncertain.

slides.question: How does Egyptian blue give away paint on statues that look bare?
options: It glows in infrared when lit
It turns green as it ages
slides.explanation: Egyptian blue gives off infrared light when lit, revealing traces of paint on surfaces that look bare to the eye.
